sections.html:
The Bitterroot Valley makes up Ravalli County, tucked into western Montana below Missoula County and against the Idaho line. Hamilton is its one city. Darby, Pinesdale and Stevensville are the towns, and Corvallis, Florence, Victor, Conner and Sula round out the map. Public land covers a big share, with parts of the Bitterroot and Lolo National Forests inside the line.

People keep arriving: 44,174 counted in 2020, then an estimate of 48,582 for 2025, about 10 percent more. With 84.4 percent of residents in rural areas, plenty of sellers live well outside the towns, and for them the treasurer and the state revenue office matter more than any city hall. Owners occupy 76.5 percent of occupied homes, and 11.0 percent of the 21,062 housing units stand vacant.

No other Montana county currently carries a higher wildfire risk to structures than Ravalli, and over 7,000 homes and structures sit at risk in the greater Bitterroot Front project area. That Forest Service project runs along the mountain front above the main valley, from McClain Creek in the north to Trapper Creek in the south, and relies on thinning, harvest and prescribed burning to cut fuel. Pockets of dense trees killed by mountain pine beetle, Douglas-fir bark beetle and western spruce budworm make the picture worse.

Near the forest edge, buyers will bring up fire risk and insurance. Selling for cash as is keeps that talk brief, since the buyer accepts the house in its present condition. Whatever route you pick, have your insurance paperwork and any brush clearing records on hand.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Ravalli County
sections.html:
Property tax here runs through two offices. The state's Department of Revenue decides what a property is worth and which class it falls in. The Ravalli County Treasurer sends bills, takes payments and chases delinquencies. Take valuation questions to the first and payment problems to the second.

Montana divides the bill into two equal parts: 5 p.m. on November 30 for the first, and 5 p.m. on May 31 of the following year for the second. Paying everything in November is allowed.

Payment eventRule
First installment5 p.m., November 30
Second installment5 p.m., May 31
Penalty and interest2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest per month (MCA 15-16-102)
Delinquent listPrinted each June, with notice that a tax lien is about to attach
Redemption window3 years after the lien attaches

Some 2026 due dates were moved, so check the date printed on your own bill with the Ravalli County Treasurer rather than assuming November 30.

Primary residences and long-term rentals are taxed in four slices for 2026, and each slice has its own percentage:

  • First $378,000 of market value: 0.76%.
  • $378,001 up to $756,000: 0.90%.
  • $756,001 up to $1,511,999: 1.10%.
  • $1,512,000 and above: 1.90%.

Cabins and other second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots all pay one flat 1.90%. On land, the rates are 2.05% for qualified agricultural land, 14.35% for non-qualified agricultural land and 0.37% for forest land, while a house and one-acre homesite on those parcels get the residential rate when lived in or rented long term. Qualifying means living there 7 or more months of 2026, or renting for 28 or more days at a time over at least 7 months.

Someone buying your house as a cabin will pay the flat rate, so your owner-occupied bill is not a safe preview of theirs.

The Department of Revenue is where an appeal begins. Within 30 days of the date on your classification and appraisal notice, send in Form AB-26, the request for informal classification and appraisal review. Values for 2025 to 2026 were set as of January 1, 2024.

Another option is the county tax appeal board. File with the county clerk and recorder inside the same 30 days. The county commissioners appoint this board, and it answers to no one at the Department of Revenue. Losing there leaves the Montana Tax Appeal Board and finally district court.

Keep paying while the dispute runs. Section 15-1-402, MCA, treats a protest as valid only if you file it in writing with the county treasurer and pay the disputed tax on time. Missing either one costs you the refund if the value drops.

Strong exhibits include your estimate of market value on the valuation date, a sale price from within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales and a builder's cost breakdown.

Back tax follows the house, not the owner. It turns into a tax lien that attaches early in August after the unpaid year, and nothing releases it until tax, interest, penalties and costs are paid in full. The county can hold on to the lien or sell it to a third party, who then gets an assignment certificate.

You hold title for three years from the day the lien attaches, and you can redeem it by paying the whole amount. Once that time ends, the lien holder may ask for a tax deed, and a public auction follows. Opening bids equal everything owed plus part of the appraised value.

Owing back tax does not block a sale. The title company pays the balance out of proceeds at closing, and the deed goes to the county clerk and recorder together with a Realty Transfer Certificate. Some owners can get help before it comes to that: the Property Tax Assistance Program for low-income Montanans, the Montana Disabled Veteran program and a land value assistance program for long-held family homes.

A practical order for a seller with arrears: ask the treasurer for the total owed, tell the title company about any lien notice you received, and ask for the payoff in writing before you accept an offer. Check whether the lien has been assigned to a third party, since that changes who gets paid.

faqs.q: When are Ravalli County property taxes due?
faqs.a: State law sets November 30 for the first half and May 31 for the second half, each at 5 p.m. Some counties moved their 2026 first-half dates, so confirm the current date with the Ravalli County Treasurer.

faqs.q: Who sets the value of my Ravalli County home?
faqs.a: The Montana Department of Revenue classifies and appraises property. The county treasurer uses the value on your classification and appraisal notice to calculate your bill.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my valuation?
faqs.a: You have 30 days from the date on your classification and appraisal notice to file Form AB-26 with the Department of Revenue, or to appeal directly to the county tax appeal board through the county clerk and recorder.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay on time?
faqs.a: A 2 percent penalty and interest of 5/6 of 1 percent per month are added. Unpaid tax becomes a lien, and after three years the lien can lead to a tax deed and a public auction.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Ravalli County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax lien stays with the property, so it must be paid or settled at closing. A cash buyer can purchase the house as is and pay the balance from the proceeds.
